stem: You need to build an AI that detects spam emails. What is the RIGHT first step?

options.text: Train a neural network immediately
Decompose the problem: what data do you need? What does 'spam' mean? How will you measure success?
Download the largest possible model from the internet
Write code first, ask questions later

explanation_after: Decomposition is the first engineering skill. Before writing a line of code: define what 'spam' means, determine what data you have, decide how to measure success.

stem: Your ML model's accuracy is 95% but the product team says it's not working. What should you investigate first?

options.text: Train for more epochs
Check if accuracy is the right metric — maybe the failure cases are the 5% that matter most
Switch to a different model architecture immediately
Collect more training data

explanation_after: 95% accuracy sounds great — until you realise the dataset is 95% non-spam and the model just says 'not spam' for everything. Always ask: Is accuracy actually what we care about here?

stem: What is the name for breaking a large problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems?

options.text: Decomposition
Compilation
Iteration
Randomisation

explanation_after: Decomposition is the core problem-solving technique in engineering. The best way to solve any hard problem is to make it not one hard problem.

stem: Before building a system to recommend products to users, which question is MOST important to answer first?

options.text: Which recommendation algorithm has the most GitHub stars?
What does 'a good recommendation' mean here — clicks? purchases? time on page — since that decides how you'll measure success
How many lines of code will the final system have?
Which programming language is fastest?

explanation_after: Before any technical choice, you must define the goal in measurable terms. Without a clear definition of success, you can't tell if any solution — simple or sophisticated — is actually working.

stem: Your data pipeline crashes on a dataset of 1 million rows, but you don't know which row is causing it. What is the most effective problem-solving strategy?

options.text: Rewrite the entire pipeline from scratch
Narrow it down by testing on progressively smaller subsets of the data to isolate which rows trigger the failure
Ignore the error and skip that step
Add more RAM to the machine

explanation_after: Isolating a problem by repeatedly narrowing the search space is far faster than blind rewriting or guessing. This 'bisection' debugging strategy is a divide-and-conquer approach, the same halving logic that makes binary search efficient.

stem: You're asked to 'build an AI that predicts customer churn.' Applying decomposition, which is the correct order of sub-problems to tackle?

options.text: Deploy a model, then collect data, then check if it works
Define what 'churn' means and gather labelled data, explore and clean the data, choose and train a model, evaluate against a clear metric, then deploy and monitor
Pick the fanciest neural network architecture, then figure out the problem later
Write the user interface first, then decide what the model should predict

explanation_after: This is the standard ML project pipeline, and it's decomposition applied at the project level: a vague goal ('predict churn') is broken into ordered sub-problems, each with a clear deliverable. Jumping straight to model architecture or deployment before defining the problem and data is one of the most common mistakes in real-world ML projects.
